newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Clinton unveils $1 billion greenhouse aid plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton unveils $1 billion greenhouse aid plan.

text.p: President Bill Clinton pledged on Thursday to cut "significantly" U.S. greenhouse gases and pledged $1 billion in aid to help developing nations reduce their production of the gases.
But the United States rejected European Union targets for sharp cuts in the gases that cause global warming as "impossible" to meet.
"To help developing nations reduce greenhouse gas emissions, the U.S. will provide them with $1 billion in assistance over the next five years," Clinton told the U.N. Earth Summit.

Most of the $1 billion aid plan will come from money already earmarked for foreign assistance. U.S. officials said $750 million would be shifted from existing foreign aid programmes, while other funds would be in loan guarantees.
Clinton said the United States, the world's biggest polluter, has clear responsibilities to control its own emissions of carbon dioxide and to help the efforts of developing nations.

"These funds will go to programmes that support energy efficiency, develop alternative energy sources and improve resource management to promote growth that does not adversely affect the climate," Clinton said.

Sensitive to the complaints of European leaders that the United States has failed to commit itself to specific reductions in carbon dioxide emissions, Clinton said he would seek specific targets when a U.N. conference on global warming meets in Kyoto, Japan at the end of the year.

"We will work with our people -- and we will bring to the Kyoto conference a strong American commitment to realistic and binding limits that will significantly reduce our emissions of greenhouse gases," Clinton said.
"Here in the United States, we must do better," Clinton said, noting "with 4 percent of the world's population, we produce 20 percent of its greenhouse gases."
"So we must do better, and we will," he said, saying "This is a challenge we must undertake immediately and one in which I personally plan to play a critical role."
Greenhouse gases that cause climate-changing global warming were one of the most contentious issues at last weekend's summit of industrialised nations in Denver.
European leaders there slammed Clinton for refusing to accept strict targets for cutting greenhouse emissions.
The G7 communique said the rich nations' club wanted clear and realistic targets for cuts but avoided the European Union target of a 15 percent reduction by the year 2010.

In a briefing before Clinton's speech, Katie McGinty, head of the White House's Council on Environmental Quality, dismissed the targets sought by the EU, saying: "It is impossible to achieve 15 to 20 percent reductions in that time period."
She said that "for the United States, those numbers are not realistic" and added, "We want to do this with the kind of seriousness of purpose that says we know that we will get there."

The Earth Summit began earlier this week with U.S. allies, like British Prime Minister Tony Blair and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, chiding Clinton for failing to show resolve in dealing with global warming.
The United States accounts for 23 percent of greenhouse gas emissions and environmentalists say all efforts to combat the problem are doomed without strong U.S. action.
Clinton said in his speech he will host a White House conference in the fall to discuss global warming and generate broad public support for eliminating greenhouse gases.
He also announced a drive to install one million solar units on the rooftops of homes and businesses throughout the United States by the year 2010.
The federal cost for the project would be about $200 million annually, acording to administration officials.
